headline: Can Cereal Be Healthy? Big Companies Are Trying.

paragraphs.text: In hindsight, this year’s fiber-forward Super Bowl commercial starring William Shatner may have been a Hail Mary. Using the nickname Will Shat, Mr. Shatner passes around boxes of Raisin Bran while making puns about bowel movements. He even name-checked a Shih Tzu.

Cereal is in trouble. Despite a brief glimmer of growth during the pandemic, the nearly $13 billion business in the United States has gone soggy. Shoppers last year bought 13 percent less cereal than in 2021, according to Nielsen IQ. Despite price hikes, dollar sales are declining, too.

At a time when gut health, protein content and convenience drive food sales, many Americans view grabbing a breakfast bar or drinkable yogurt — or nothing at all — as easier and healthier than pouring milk over a bowl of ultraprocessed grains from a box. Younger people didn’t grow up with the same cultural or emotional attachment to breakfast cereals as earlier generations raised on cereal ads sandwiched between Saturday-morning cartoons.

“Generation Z in particular is not so enthusiastic about cereal for breakfast, and that’s hit the long-established players in the market,” said Richard Caines, a senior analyst with the market research company Mintel. “They are more enthusiastic about products that have functional health benefits.”

Mix in pressure from the “Make America Healthy Again” movement’s push for less-processed food, in addition to the rise of GLP-1 drugs and higher prices for what used to be a budget-stretcher, and you can understand why cereal executives are worried.

As it has many times since the first bowl was poured during the Lincoln administration, the industry is returning to cereal’s roots as a health food, born of a Victorian belief that bland grains softened in milk could restart sluggish digestive tracts and ease other maladies.

Classic cereal boxes are being redesigned to trumpet their fiber and vitamin content, or reformulated with more protein and less sugar. Granola is the new It cereal. In July, WK Kellogg Co., which the food giant Ferrero Group bought in 2025, introduced Kashi Gut Health Granola. A month later, Ferrero bought Purely Elizabeth, a granola company started by a Manhattan holistic-nutrition counselor, for $850 million.

“Now is the time to be deliberate and disruptive in continuing to make cereal culturally relevant,” said Doug VanDeVelde, chief growth officer at WK Kellogg, in May as the company rolled out a redesign for some cereals that covers a third of the box with simplified nutrition information, highlighting the ingredients in vogue with health-focused shoppers.

“Consumers are telling us that they want their cereal to work harder for them and to do more,” said Joan Kavanaugh, vice president for national buying of the global discount supermarket chain Aldi. “And while it does more for them, it needs to cost less.”
Like other grocery companies with their own private-label lines, Aldi is creating new cereals with added protein and fiber.

The four biggest cereal companies, which control about 80 percent of the market, are feeling pressure from the growing popularity of those house brands and from small protein-forward, no-sugar upstarts like Catalina Crunch and Magic Spoon, which began selling only online and are now in thousands of supermarkets.
Sweetening Sales

For all that, the towering wall of cereal boxes in any store is still dominated by Cinnamon Toast Crunch, Frosted Flakes and other sugary favorites that cereal makers euphemistically call “taste-forward cereals.”
But even those are getting a glow-up.

The Ghost supplement company joined General Mills this year to create a Lucky Charms-flavored cereal with 17 grams of protein per serving, which is a cup and a quarter. That’s more than four times the amount in the original version, with about 25 percent less sugar. A banner promising “high fiber to support digestive wellness” has been slapped across boxes of Frosted Mini-Wheats. Cheerios Cookies & Crème with Protein, which General Mills infused with protein powder from yellow peas, is a top seller on Instacart.

“It’s all about macros,” said Laura Jones, Instacart’s chief marketing officer, referring to macronutrients like proteins, carbohydrates and fats. “We’re looking for the intersection of health goals plus the emotional level of fulfillment that you can get from a comfort food like cereal.”
Four of the top 10 fastest-growing cereals on the Instacart site are high-protein, and three of those are versions of Cheerios.

Alyssa Buckalew, vice president for innovation, technology and quality at General Mills, said Americans still love cereal. “The category has been challenged and there’s a number of reasons for that, but we do feel that there’s still relevance for cereal,” she said.

Like other big cereal companies, General Mills is trying to entice more adults to eat its sugar-laden cereals, like Golden Grahams and Lucky Charms, with the message that they’re not just for breakfast. Cereal is being promoted as a dessert with benefits. It now comes packaged in tubes or individual pouches that can be tipped directly into the mouth — leaving, say, a gamer’s hands free of crumbs.

Last spring, Dairy Queen introduced shakes made with Fruity Pebbles and cones covered in crushed Cinnamon Toast Crunch called “cinnadust.” Kellogg’s has even started putting toys back in cereal boxes.
A Pantry Full of Kashi
Nyles Peterson and Megan Saia are exactly the health-focused customers the cereal makers aim for. The Atlanta couple bake focaccia on the weekends and think a lot about their macros.

Ms. Saia, 28, a lawyer, never ate cereal while growing up and didn’t think she ever would. Mr. Peterson, 31, an engineer, loved Cinnamon Toast Crunch so much that his friends sent him a carton of it as a joke when he was in college. His tastes have matured along with his health goals.
“Eating a bowl of cereal is pretty fast and easy and enjoyable,” he said. “To get protein and fiber from it is a big plus.”

They tried psyllium husks and other sources of fiber, but didn’t love the taste or how it made them feel. They hunted for a cereal with a simple list of ingredients, lots of fiber and none of the whey or pea protein add-ins that can give it a peculiar taste and texture.
Their mainstay is Kashi GO Original, whose 12 grams each of protein and fiber per serving are big selling points. More than a dozen boxes of various Kashi cereals sit in their pantry.

“Initially I didn’t want to eat it because I thought it was ultraprocessed, which I’m sure it is,” Ms. Saia said. “But it’s just so convenient and an easy way to get enough fiber that I don’t really care, and it makes me feel fine.”

They eat it with yogurt, whole milk or as a dry snack. And because cereal prices have risen about 25 percent since 2020, according to data from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, they wait for buy-one, get-one sales to load up their cart.
Back to the Beginning

Breakfast cereal as we know it was created in 1863 by Dr. James Caleb Jackson, a physician in a Western New York sanitarium. His recipe was a dried mix of water and a coarse whole wheat flour championed by Sylvester Graham, an eccentric, health-obsessed Presbyterian minister who invented the graham cracker.

Dr. Jackson named his cereal granula, and it was so hard you couldn’t eat it unless it soaked overnight in milk or water. He and other evangelists for better nutrition believed that bland, unstimulating food would soothe the body’s digestive system and suppress sexual urges.

Two brothers, John Harvey Kellogg and Will Keith Kellogg, who were influenced by the dietary edicts of Seventh-Day Adventism and ran a sanitarium in Battle Creek, Mich., came up with cornflakes 35 years later. Around the same time, the businessman Charles William Post created Grape-Nuts.

Decades of advertising, food-science advances and mountains of sugar followed, transforming cereal into what the nutritionist Marion Nestle calls “vitamin-supplemented cookies” in her new book, “Sugar Coated: Unboxing the Hidden Forces Shaping America’s Favorite Breakfast Food.”

She wrote it with Lisa Sutherland, a former vice president for nutrition at the Kellogg Company and the interim president of Jacksonville University. “The more things change, the more things stay the same in the cereal industry,” Dr. Sutherland said. “They just keep cycling back to their roots.”

Cereal companies, which might introduce a dozen varieties of their most popular cereals every year, have two ways to catch a health wave. They can redesign packaging to emphasize certain nutrients that already exist, a process that can take a few months, or change the formula. That’s trickier, and can take a year or longer.

“When you change or add certain ingredients, they can have funky flavors to them,” Dr. Sutherland said. Vitamin D can add a metallic taste, and certain proteins lend a bitter or cardboard flavor and a chalky texture. “So then you have to figure out how am I going to mask the flavor and deal with the structural impact.”
Claims and Clashes

Companies most often turn to linguistic gymnastics to give their cereal a health halo, sometimes battling federal regulators and consumer groups. The fights come down to minuscule details like the font size on labels, the definition of words like healthy and nutritious, or larger scientific questions like whether cereal really can help you sleep better, improve a child’s attentiveness or prevent a heart attack.
In 1984, Kellogg partnered with the National Cancer Institute to claim that the fiber in cereal might prevent colon cancer.
“Once that happened, there was no going back,” Dr. Nestle writes. “Kellogg hadn’t discussed it with the F.D.A., and its officials were appalled. But the National Cancer Institute was thrilled.”

The most famous battle between cereal companies and the Food and Drug Administration came in the late 2000s, when General Mills mounted a vast marketing campaign claiming that the oat fiber in Cheerios could lower cholesterol by 4 percent in six weeks. The F.D.A. said that promoting the cereal with specific, clinically proven medical outcomes effectively reclassified Cheerios as an unapproved new drug under federal law. The company reverted to more generic claims, like “can help lower cholesterol.”
“If you give it a moment’s thought,” Dr. Nestle said, “you know that proving breakfast cereal prevents heart disease is ridiculous.”

To her mind, the worst misrepresentation came during the 2009 swine flu epidemic, when Kellogg executives added a prominent “immunity” banner on boxes of Rice Krispies and Cocoa Krispies, claiming that the cereals’ antioxidants could help keep children from getting sick.

Nutritionists and consumer watchdog groups called the move predatory and deceptive, pointing out that refined grain cereals that were nearly 40 percent sugar by weight weren’t exactly health foods. State attorneys general balked, and the Federal Trade Commission barred Kellogg from making health or immunity benefit claims unless they were backed by scientific evidence.
“They’re just desperate to find a way to sell,” Dr. Nestle said. “They never miss a trick.”
